'''''Phalaris aquatica''''', known by the common names '''bulbous canary-grass'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> and '''Harding grass''', is a species of grass in the genus ''[[Phalaris (plant)|Phalaris]]'' of the family [[Poaceae]].

==Description==
It is an erect, waist-high, stout perennial [[bunch grass]], with grayish to bluish green leaves. Flowering heads are dense, spike-like, and usually {{convert|2 to 5|in|round=5}} long. It is slow to develop from seed, but can form large bunches after several years.<ref name="Cal-IPC">{{cite web | title=''Phalaris aquatica'' | website=[[California Invasive Plant Council]] | date=2006-02-06 | url=http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=67&surveynumber=182 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060206095002/http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=67&surveynumber=182 | archive-date=2006-02-06 | access-date=2022-05-03}}</ref>

''[[Phalaris arundinacea]]'' (reed canary grass) differs from Harding grass in having more distinct rhizomes, and an inflorescence that is compact at first but becomes more open as the branches spread.

Hybrids of Harding grass and reed canary grass have been produced.  Varieties include 'AQ1', 'Uneta', and 'Australis'.

''P. aquatica'' is a quick-growing grass which incorporates and utilises soil nitrogen rapidly.<ref name="Cheplick-1998">{{cite conference | editor-last=Cheplick | editor-first=Gregory Paul | publisher=[[Botanical Society of America]] ([[Cambridge University Press|CUP]]) | title=Population Biology of Grasses | publication-place=New York | isbn=978-0-511-52544-5 | oclc=847373775 | doi=10.1017/CBO9780511525445 | publication-date=1998 | date=8 August 1995 | conference=Annual meeting of the Botanical Society of America | location=[[San Diego]], California, USA | pages=xii–399}}</ref>{{rp|pages=169–174}}

==Geography==
''Phalaris aquatica'' originated from [[Southern Europe]] and the [[Caucasus]]. It is naturalized in South Africa, Australia, New Zealand and the United States.<ref name=heuze2017>{{cite web|author1=Heuzé V.|author2=Tran G.|author3=Boudon A.|author4=Lebas F.|date=2017|title=Bulbous canary grass (''Phalaris aquatica'')|website=Feedipedia.org|url=https://www.feedipedia.org/node/391}}</ref> Although very recently introduced there, its [[pasture]] value was first recognised in Australia.<ref name="Oram-et-al-2009">{{cite journal | last1=Oram | first1=R. N. | last2=Ferreira | first2=V. | last3=Culvenor | first3=R. A. | last4=Hopkins | first4=A. A. | last5=Stewart | first5=A. | title=The first century of ''Phalaris aquatica'' L. cultivation and genetic improvement: a review | journal=[[Crop & Pasture Science]] | publisher=[[CSIRO Publishing|CSIRO]] | volume=60 | issue=1 | year=2009 | page=1 | issn=1836-0947 | doi=10.1071/cp08170 | s2cid=83767465}}</ref> Domesticated cultivation then spread to the United States, Argentina and several other countries in South America, and New Zealand.<ref name="Oram-et-al-2009" />

== Constituents ==
''Phalaris aquatica'' contains a variety of secondary metabolites, primarily indole and tryptamine alkaloids, which are implicated in livestock toxicity.<ref name="AbdElmaseh2024">{{cite journal |last1=Abd-Elmaseh |first1=Eriny Talat |last2=Samy |first2=Mamdouh Nabil |last3=Abdelkader |first3=Mohamed Salah Eldein |last4=Fouad |first4=Mostafa Ahmed |title=A review of phytoconstituents and biological activities of genus Phalaris |journal=Journal of Advanced Biomedical and Pharmaceutical Sciences |year=2024 |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=80–87 |doi=10.21608/jabps.2024.263051.1179}}</ref>

==Forage==
''Phalaris aquatica'' is a pasture species grazed by ruminants. The grass can also be cut, providing good quality fodder for grazing livestock for 8 to 12 months a year.<ref name="heuze2017" />

==Toxicity==
Some ''Phalaris'' species contain [[gramine]] (also found in Avena sativa 'Oats') which is claimed to cause brain damage, other organ damage, [[central nervous system]] damage and death in sheep (when injected in very large amounts).<ref name="some_book_gramine">

[[Image:Phalaris-aquatica-seeds.jpg|thumb|right|Seeds]]

In [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], Australia, it is reported that [[kangaroos]] grazing on ''Phalaris aquatica'' may develop a condition known familiarly as "Phalaris staggers", in which coordination and mobility are affected.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-06-21/grass-to-blame-for-staggering-kangaroos/9886884|title=Kangaroos under the influence: Grass to blame for staggering death of 'drunken' kangaroos |first1=Jo |last1=Printz |first2=Mark |last2=Kearney |date=21 June 2018 |work=ABC News |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=29 November 2021}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
Harding grass is an [[invasive species]] in [[grassland]], [[California oak woodland|oak woodland]], [[chaparral]], and [[riparian zone|riparian]] [[habitat]]s. Native grasses and grassland habitat in California are affected.{{citation needed|date=June 2022}}
